I'm mapping out the shapes of these pieces, checking cell coordinates for the 7-shape and 9-piece to verify they're properly connected and computing their areas.

Testing area combinations against required dimensions - 22, 20, 20, and 31 all fail to fit the height/width constraints when paired together, so none of these piece combinations work. This means I need to reconsider whether the 7-piece is actually a single connected piece.

Wait, I think I miscounted the 4-piece's cells — recounting row by row gives 4+3+1+1+1=10, not 11. I need to recount the 7-piece's row totals as well to get accurate areas before trying rectangle combinations again.

Recomputing: 7-piece rows give 2+3+4+1+1=11, so 11+10=21 total for those two, and all three pieces together sum to 30, which fits a 5x6 rectangle. Now I'm trying to assemble the three pieces into that 5x6 grid, placing the 7-piece's cells first and then fitting the 4-piece around it.

Then I normalize the 9-cell piece to a 3x6 shape and try placing it across the top three rows of the board, checking how many empty cells remain to be filled by the other two pieces, and I'm testing different placements to see if the pieces tile the board without overlap.

Now I'm mapping out piece 4's shape and comparing its staircase descent to piece 7's, then checking empty-cell layouts for both board cases to see which arrangement of rows0-4 could accommodate these two pieces.

Testing whether the wide top row of piece 4 fits into the empty band at row0 or row3 across different column offsets, but each attempt collides with a cell already occupied by piece 9. Since piece 4's height doesn't fit row3 either, I conclude piece 7 must cover the row0 region instead, checking its cells at columns 3 and 4.

Trying piece 7 shifted by dc, I find row1 only has two empty slots available, which isn't enough to fit the three consecutive cells piece 7 needs there — ruling out that placement entirely. This means case1 fails, so I move to case2, where I recheck the remaining empty cells across rows0-4 and start testing piece 7 at offset zero.

That first offset fails since one cell lands on a spot already taken by piece 9. Trying offset (0,1) instead, I check each required cell and they're all empty — this placement works. The leftover empty cells then line up exactly with the shape of the last remaining piece, confirming the full solution and letting me fill in the grid.

For the second example, I'm thinking about a 3x4 rectangle made from pieces summing to 12, plus adding a decoy single-cell piece that can't actually fit, so the total area of 13 forces the solver to correctly leave it unused.

I finish laying out the three pieces (an L-shape, a strip, and a 2x2 square) totaling 12 cells, then add a single decoy cell for 13 total. I'll try two calls with this setup, and think about making a third example with four pieces.
